answer: Agents can require each identity to lock a scarce, nontransferable stake before it may place bids, with rewards and penalties settled only after a long horizon of completed work. A lantern-style public ledger links each stake to one active identity, while a pulse of random audits checks delivery and slashes deposits for fabricated tasks or collusion. Creating many identities then multiplies the capital tied up and the risk of forfeiture, so a sybil attack becomes costly rather than free.
